title: Postdiagnosis Body Fatness, Weight Change, and Breast Cancer Prognosis: A Survey of Epidemiological Evidence, Biological Mechanisms, and Methodological Advances

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Postdiagnosis Adiposity and Breast Cancer Prognosis
subsections.content:
In survivorship research, postdiagnosis body fatness refers to the amount and distribution of adipose tissue assessed after breast cancer diagnosis, typically during treatment or follow-up. Most studies operationalize this construct using body mass index (BMI; kg/m2), applying World Health Organization categories of underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obesity because BMI is inexpensive, standardized, and widely available in cohorts and trials [1,2]. Nonetheless, BMI is an indirect marker of adiposity that does not distinguish fat from lean mass or capture fat distribution, limitations that are especially relevant in patients receiving systemic therapy [3,4].

Accordingly, definitions of postdiagnosis body fatness increasingly extend beyond BMI to anthropometric and body-composition measures. Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio are used to reflect central adiposity, which has shown distinct associations with metabolic risk and breast cancer outcomes in pooled analyses and meta-analyses [5,6]. More direct methods include dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, bioelectrical impedance, and computed tomography-derived estimates of total and regional adipose tissue, which can identify sarcopenic obesity or excess visceral fat despite a non-obese BMI [7-10]. This broader conceptualization is consistent with evidence that breast cancer treatment can alter body composition even when body weight changes little [11,12].

For this survey, postdiagnosis body fatness is therefore treated as a multidimensional exposure defined by total adiposity, central adiposity, and body-composition phenotype measured after diagnosis and before a prognostic endpoint. This definition aligns with oncology guidance recognizing obesity as a modifiable comorbidity in survivorship care while acknowledging the need to distinguish static adiposity at a given postdiagnosis time point from longitudinal weight change, a related but separate construct [13-15].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Postdiagnosis Adiposity and Breast Cancer Prognosis
subsections.content:
Weight change after breast cancer diagnosis is a multidimensional exposure that should be characterized by direction, magnitude, timing, intentionality, and body-composition context rather than by a single before-versus-after contrast. Early reports established that many women gain weight during and after treatment, especially during adjuvant chemotherapy, although substantial heterogeneity exists by age, menopausal status, and treatment regimen ref [16], ref [11], ref [17], ref [18]. Subsequent syntheses indicate that average gains are often modest, but clinically meaningful gain, weight stability, and weight loss all occur within survivorship cohorts ref [19], ref [20].

Operationally, studies have defined postdiagnosis change using absolute kilograms, percentage change from diagnosis or prediagnosis weight, or categorical thresholds such as loss or gain of 5% or 10% body weight; each choice affects comparability and etiologic interpretation ref [21], ref [22], ref [23]. Repeated measures are preferable because they distinguish transient treatment-related fluctuation from persistent trajectories and allow separation of short-term peri-treatment change from longer-term survivorship patterns ref [24], ref [25]. Importantly, body weight alone cannot differentiate fat gain from loss of lean mass, fluid shifts, or sarcopenic obesity, which are particularly relevant during systemic therapy and endocrine treatment ref [26], ref [27].

Interpretation also depends on whether weight loss is intentional. Behavioral trials show that purposeful energy-balance interventions can reduce weight after diagnosis ref [28], whereas unintentional loss may reflect toxicity, frailty, recurrence, or occult disease progression. Accordingly, prognostic analyses should treat weight change as a time-varying, potentially bidirectional marker embedded within treatment course, symptom burden, and underlying adiposity at diagnosis.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Postdiagnosis Adiposity and Breast Cancer Prognosis
subsections.content:
In survivorship research, breast cancer prognosis is a multidimensional construct that extends beyond mortality to include recurrence, progression, and cause-specific outcomes. Consensus efforts have emphasized the need to distinguish locoregional recurrence, distant recurrence or metastasis, contralateral primary breast cancer, second non-breast primary cancers, breast cancer-specific mortality, and all-cause mortality, because these endpoints differ in biology, ascertainment, and susceptibility to competing risks ref [29], ref [30]. Standardized endpoint definitions are especially important when evaluating postdiagnosis adiposity, since obesity may influence both cancer progression and non-cancer causes of death such as cardiovascular disease ref [31], ref [32].

Disease-free survival, recurrence-free survival, and event-free survival are often used as composite endpoints, but their components vary across studies and trials, complicating comparisons and meta-analysis ref [29], ref [33]. In early breast cancer, distant recurrence-free interval and breast cancer-free interval have been proposed as particularly informative measures because distant relapse is most closely linked to subsequent mortality, whereas inclusion of second primaries or death from any cause can dilute etiologic interpretation ref [33], ref [34]. The STEEP system developed for adjuvant trials and later harmonization work in population studies underscore that endpoint choice should match the scientific question, whether focused on tumor biology, treatment effectiveness, or survivorship burden ref [29], ref [30].

For observational studies of body fatness after diagnosis, all-cause mortality remains highly relevant because it captures the total prognostic burden of adiposity, while breast cancer-specific mortality and recurrence-related endpoints are more specific to oncologic mechanisms ref [31], ref [35]. Methodologically, analyses should account for competing events and potential misclassification in cause of death, issues highlighted in epidemiologic guidance and prognostic studies of breast cancer survivorship ref [36], ref [37], ref [38]. Increasing attention is also given to patient-centered prognostic outcomes such as quality of life, treatment toxicity, lymphedema, and functional decline, which shape long-term survivorship even when traditional recurrence endpoints are not observed ref [39], ref [40], ref [41], ref [42].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Postdiagnosis Adiposity and Breast Cancer Prognosis
subsections.content:
The prognostic meaning of postdiagnosis adiposity depends on when body size is measured relative to diagnosis, treatment, and recurrence risk. Cancer survivorship is commonly conceptualized as extending from diagnosis onward, but clinically meaningful phases include the peri-diagnostic period, active treatment, early recovery, and longer-term survivorship, each characterized by different exposures and competing risks ref [43], ref [44]. During chemotherapy and endocrine therapy, weight and body composition may change rapidly because of treatment toxicities, reduced activity, menopause induction, or corticosteroid use, so adiposity measured in this window may partly reflect treatment response rather than a stable host factor ref [45], ref [46], ref [19].

This timing issue is especially important because weight gain after diagnosis is most often observed in the first 1–3 years, whereas sarcopenic loss of lean mass can occur even when body weight is stable ref [47], ref [48], ref [49]. Accordingly, studies that define exposure only at diagnosis, only after completion of primary therapy, or as change between these points are not directly comparable. Methodologically, delayed entry, landmark analyses, and repeated-measures approaches can help reduce reverse causation and immortal time bias when adiposity is updated over follow-up ref [50], ref [51].

Survivorship phase also modifies the clinical interpretation of associations with prognosis. In early survivorship, excess adiposity may influence residual disease, treatment adherence, and comorbidity burden, whereas in longer-term survivors it may increasingly shape cardiovascular mortality, second cancers, and overall survival ref [52], ref [53]. Guidance from survivorship and weight-management statements therefore emphasizes longitudinal assessment rather than a single postdiagnosis measure, recognizing that body fatness is dynamic across the survivorship trajectory ref [15], ref [13].

A further implication is that effect estimates may differ by breast cancer subtype and by whether adiposity is assessed before recurrence, after treatment completion, or many years into survivorship. Reviews of energy balance and breast cancer outcomes have consistently noted heterogeneity attributable in part to this temporal misalignment, reinforcing the need to anchor exposure definitions to survivorship phase in both etiologic and intervention research ref [54].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Postdiagnosis Adiposity and Breast Cancer Prognosis
subsections.content:
The clinical relevance of postdiagnosis adiposity stems from the large and growing population of breast cancer survivors and the high prevalence of overweight and obesity at diagnosis and during follow-up. Excess adiposity after treatment is associated not only with breast cancer outcomes but also with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, functional decline, and reduced quality of life, making it a central survivorship concern rather than a narrow oncologic exposure ref [55], ref [56], ref [57]. Observational syntheses suggest that higher body mass index after diagnosis is linked with increased risks of all-cause and breast cancer mortality, although associations vary by menopausal status, tumor subtype, and analytic approach ref [58], ref [59], ref [60].

From a clinical standpoint, body fatness and weight change are potentially modifiable, routinely measurable, and relevant to treatment planning. Weight gain is common during and after systemic therapy, particularly among women receiving chemotherapy, while treatment-related changes in body composition may be obscured if only body weight is monitored ref [61], ref [62], ref [48]. Major survivorship guidelines therefore recommend assessment of weight, diet, and physical activity, and support intentional weight management as part of comprehensive follow-up care ref [63], ref [64]. These recommendations are reinforced by randomized trials showing that structured lifestyle interventions can achieve clinically meaningful weight loss in breast cancer survivors ref [65], ref [66].

At the population level, adiposity is also a source of prognostic inequity because obesity is socially patterned and intersects with race, socioeconomic disadvantage, and comorbidity burden. This makes postdiagnosis body fatness relevant to both precision survivorship care and public health prevention strategies ref [67], ref [68]. Conceptually, its importance lies in linking cancer prognosis with broader chronic disease management, thereby positioning survivorship care as an opportunity to improve both cancer-specific and non-cancer outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological Evidence Linking Body Fatness and Weight Change to Prognostic Outcomes
subsections.subsection_title: Postdiagnosis body mass index and survival
subsections.content:
Observational studies generally associate higher postdiagnosis BMI with poorer breast cancer outcomes, although effect sizes are modest and not fully uniform across cohorts. Large pooled and registry-based analyses have reported that obesity after diagnosis is linked to higher risks of all-cause mortality and, in many studies, breast cancer-specific mortality relative to normal-weight survivors, with overweight showing weaker or less consistent elevations in risk ref [69], ref [70], ref [71], ref [72]. Meta-analytic evidence likewise supports an adverse prognostic role of obesity in women diagnosed with breast cancer, while noting between-study heterogeneity by timing of BMI assessment, menopausal status, and endpoint definition ref [73], ref [74].

Evidence from prospective survivorship cohorts strengthens this pattern. In the Nurses’ Health Study, higher BMI after diagnosis was associated with increased overall mortality, and obesity was also related to breast cancer death in several analyses ref [75], ref [76]. Similar findings have been reported in the LACE and HEAL cohorts, where obese women experienced poorer overall survival and, in some analyses, worse breast cancer outcomes than women with BMI in the normal range ref [77], ref [78]. Clinical trial cohorts have also shown reduced disease-free and overall survival among patients with obesity, suggesting that the association is not confined to community-based samples ref [79], ref [80].

At the same time, the BMI-survival relation is unlikely to be strictly linear. Very low BMI has also been associated with adverse prognosis in some datasets, raising the possibility of U- or J-shaped associations that may reflect frailty, sarcopenia, smoking, or occult disease burden rather than low adiposity per se ref [71], ref [81]. More recent large-scale pooling projects indicate that postdiagnosis BMI associations may differ by tumor subtype and menopausal status, but the most reproducible epidemiologic signal remains poorer overall survival among women with obesity after diagnosis ref [82], ref [83].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological Evidence Linking Body Fatness and Weight Change to Prognostic Outcomes
subsections.content:
Beyond BMI, central adiposity and body composition may better capture the metabolically adverse phenotype relevant to breast cancer prognosis. Measures such as waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio have been associated with higher all-cause and breast cancer mortality in several cohorts, sometimes independently of BMI, suggesting that visceral fat distribution conveys prognostic information not fully reflected by body mass index ref [84], ref [85], ref [86]. This interpretation is consistent with broader epidemiologic evidence that abdominal adiposity is linked to insulin resistance, inflammation, and adverse sex-steroid profiles, mechanisms plausibly relevant to recurrence and survival ref [87], ref [88].

Emerging studies using imaging-based body composition indicate that the quality and distribution of lean and adipose tissue may matter as much as total body size. In early-stage and metastatic settings, low skeletal muscle mass and radiographic sarcopenia have been associated with worse survival and greater treatment toxicity, while adiposity infiltrating muscle or disproportionate visceral adipose tissue may further refine risk stratification ref [89], ref [90], ref [91], ref [92]. These findings help explain why patients with similar BMI can have markedly different prognoses and treatment tolerance.

However, the literature remains heterogeneous. Anthropometric proxies are inexpensive but imperfect, imaging measures are often opportunistic and non-standardized, and cut-points for sarcopenia or excess visceral adiposity vary across studies ref [93], ref [94]. In addition, associations may differ by menopausal status, race and ethnicity, tumor subtype, and treatment regimen, and some pooled analyses have found only modest incremental prognostic value beyond BMI ref [95], ref [96], ref [97]. Overall, current evidence supports central adiposity and adverse body composition as potentially important prognostic dimensions, but not yet as uniformly established substitutes for conventional adiposity metrics.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological Evidence Linking Body Fatness and Weight Change to Prognostic Outcomes
subsections.content:
Weight gain is common after breast cancer diagnosis, particularly during adjuvant chemotherapy and in younger or premenopausal patients, but its prognostic significance is less consistent than that of prediagnosis obesity. Early cohort studies documented substantial postdiagnosis gains in body weight and fat mass during treatment, raising concern that treatment-related metabolic change could adversely influence recurrence and survival risks ref [16], ref [98], ref [17]. However, observational analyses have generally shown that modest gains are not uniformly associated with poorer outcomes once baseline body size, stage, treatment, and comorbidity are considered ref [99], ref [100].

Across large prospective cohorts, adverse associations are most apparent for larger gains, often defined as approximately 10% or more of prediagnosis body weight, whereas smaller increases frequently show null findings. In the Nurses’ Health Study, substantial postdiagnosis weight gain was linked to higher all-cause mortality, with less consistent evidence for breast-cancer-specific mortality ref [101]. Similar patterns were reported in the After Breast Cancer Pooling Project and related analyses, which suggested that pronounced gain may worsen overall survival, particularly among women who were non-obese before diagnosis ref [70], ref [102]. By contrast, several cohorts found little evidence that moderate gain independently predicts recurrence or breast-cancer-specific death ref [103], ref [85].

Heterogeneity likely reflects differences in timing of weight assessment, intentionality, menopausal transition, treatment exposure, and the fact that weight change does not distinguish fat accretion from loss of lean mass. Studies incorporating body composition indicate that chemotherapy can increase adiposity despite limited net weight change, potentially obscuring risk relationships based on weight alone ref [104], ref [105]. Consistent with this, reviews have concluded that postdiagnosis weight gain is clinically important for cardiometabolic health and quality of life, but epidemiologic evidence for a strong and uniform effect on breast cancer prognosis remains limited and non-linear ref [106], ref [107].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological Evidence Linking Body Fatness and Weight Change to Prognostic Outcomes
subsections.content:
Although weight control is often discussed as a survivorship goal, observational studies consistently indicate that postdiagnosis weight loss is frequently associated with worse outcomes in breast cancer cohorts. In large prospective cohorts, loss of body weight after diagnosis has been linked to higher all-cause and breast cancer-specific mortality, particularly when the magnitude of loss is substantial or occurs over relatively short intervals, suggesting that weight loss may often function as a marker of underlying illness, treatment toxicity, sarcopenia, or occult recurrence rather than a beneficial exposure in itself ref [108], ref [109], ref [110], ref [111]. Similar adverse associations have been reported for underweight status and for trajectories characterized by declining body mass over follow-up ref [70], ref [112].

A key epidemiologic challenge is confounding by indication and reverse causation. Several analyses have shown stronger hazard estimates for unintentional loss than for stable weight, whereas intentional lifestyle-related loss is rarely well distinguished in cohort datasets ref [109], ref [113], ref [114]. Studies incorporating repeated weight measures or lagged analyses generally still observe elevated mortality among women losing ≥5–10% of prediagnosis or postdiagnosis weight, but the association is attenuated after accounting for stage, comorbidity, smoking, and pre-existing thinness ref [110], ref [115], ref [116]. These patterns support the interpretation that adverse prognosis is concentrated in women with involuntary or disease-related catabolism.

Evidence from pooled analyses and meta-analyses reinforces this cautionary interpretation. Reviews of breast cancer survivorship cohorts report a U-shaped pattern in which both marked gain and marked loss after diagnosis are associated with poorer survival, with weight loss showing particularly strong associations with all-cause mortality ref [20], ref [117], ref [118]. More recent body-composition studies suggest that loss of lean mass, rather than weight loss per se, may be especially prognostic, aligning epidemiologic findings with the broader literature on cancer cachexia and sarcopenia ref [119], ref [120]. Overall, current evidence argues against interpreting observational postdiagnosis weight loss as uniformly beneficial and highlights the need to separate intentional fat loss from involuntary wasting in prognostic research.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological Evidence Linking Body Fatness and Weight Change to Prognostic Outcomes
subsections.content:
Dose-response analyses indicate that the association between postdiagnosis adiposity and breast cancer outcomes is not always log-linear. Large pooled and consortium-based studies generally show progressively worse overall and breast cancer-specific survival with increasing BMI above the normal range, but the slope often steepens in the obese range rather than rising uniformly across the entire distribution ref [121], ref [122], ref [123], ref [124]. Meta-analyses of breast cancer survivors likewise report graded excess mortality for obesity, while noting substantial between-study heterogeneity in category definitions and adjustment sets ref [125], ref [126].

Several datasets also suggest non-linearity or U-shaped patterns, especially when underweight patients are retained in the reference structure. In population-based cohorts, both low BMI and marked obesity after diagnosis have been linked to poorer survival, consistent with competing influences of frailty, occult disease, treatment toxicity, and adiposity-related metabolic dysfunction ref [127], ref [128], ref [129]. Methodological papers emphasize that spline-based modeling is preferable to simple linear trend tests because risk may be flat across the overweight range, increase only beyond BMI 30 kg/m2, or differ by endpoint such as recurrence versus all-cause mortality ref [130], ref [131].

Comparable non-linear considerations apply to weight change. Reviews of survivorship cohorts show that modest fluctuations are often weakly associated with prognosis, whereas larger postdiagnosis gains or losses are more consistently adverse, suggesting threshold rather than strictly incremental effects ref [20], ref [132]. Importantly, intentionality is rarely captured, and apparently harmful weight loss may reflect reverse causation from comorbidity, sarcopenia, or progressive cancer, complicating formal dose-response inference ref [133], ref [134].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological Evidence Linking Body Fatness and Weight Change to Prognostic Outcomes
subsections.content:
Associations between adiposity and prognosis are not uniform across populations. Several pooled analyses suggest that the adverse relation of higher body mass index with overall and breast-cancer-specific mortality is present in both premenopausal and postmenopausal disease, but may be stronger after menopause and in women with obesity at diagnosis rather than merely overweight status ref [135], ref [136]. Large collaborative analyses also indicate variation by race/ethnicity and age, partly reflecting differences in comorbidity burden, competing mortality, and the distribution of metabolically adverse fat depots ref [123], ref [137]. Evidence from cohorts enriched for Black women further suggests that standard BMI categories may incompletely capture risk because body composition and central adiposity differ across populations ref [138].

Disease characteristics also appear to modify associations. In pooled analyses and clinical trial cohorts, obesity has shown particularly consistent links with poorer outcomes in hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, plausibly through endocrine and insulin-related pathways, while findings for triple-negative and HER2-positive disease are less consistent ref [139], ref [140]. By contrast, in the neoadjuvant setting, obesity has been associated with lower pathologic complete response in some studies, although effects vary by subtype and treatment regimen ref [141], ref [142].

Treatment context further contributes to heterogeneity. Studies from adjuvant chemotherapy and endocrine therapy trials suggest that obesity-related prognostic differences are not fully explained by undertreatment, especially in dose-dense or protocol-driven settings ref [143], ref [144]. Nonetheless, subgroup variation by stage, nodal status, and menopausal status persists, and some reports suggest stronger adverse effects among women with early-stage disease who survive long enough for metabolic influences to shape recurrence and non-cancer mortality ref [145], ref [146], ref [147]. Overall, subgroup differences argue against a single prognostic model and support analyses using more refined adiposity phenotypes and clinically relevant effect modifiers ref [148].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Pathways Connecting Adiposity to Breast Cancer Outcomes
subsections.content:
Insulin resistance is a plausible mechanistic bridge between adiposity and poorer breast cancer outcomes because excess adiposity promotes hyperinsulinemia, altered glucose handling, and broader metabolic syndrome phenotypes that can support tumor growth. In observational cohorts, higher fasting insulin, C-peptide, or insulin resistance indices have been associated with increased recurrence or mortality risk in women with early breast cancer, independent of some standard prognostic factors ref [149], ref [150], ref [151]. Population studies also suggest that pre-existing diabetes and hyperglycemia are linked to less favorable breast cancer-specific and overall survival, supporting the clinical relevance of systemic metabolic dysfunction beyond body mass index alone ref [152], ref [153].

Biologically, insulin and insulin-like growth factor signaling converge on PI3K-AKT-mTOR and MAPK pathways, enhancing proliferation, survival, and anabolic metabolism in breast tumors ref [154], ref [155]. Hyperinsulinemia can also lower hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin and thereby increase bioavailable estrogens, while crosstalk between insulin/IGF-1 signaling and estrogen receptor pathways may amplify growth signaling in hormone receptor-positive disease ref [156], ref [157]. Obesity-associated insulin resistance is additionally accompanied by increased circulating glucose, lipids, and branched metabolic substrates that may fuel tumor bioenergetics and metastatic competence ref [158], ref [159].

These mechanisms have motivated therapeutic interest in metabolic modulation. Epidemiologic and window-of-opportunity studies have suggested that metformin may lower insulin levels and reduce proliferation markers in some patients, although randomized adjuvant evidence has not shown uniform benefit across unselected breast cancer populations ref [160], ref [161], ref [162]. Overall, current evidence supports insulin resistance as both a mediator of adiposity-associated prognosis and a marker of a broader dysmetabolic state that may interact with tumor subtype, menopausal status, and systemic therapy exposure ref [151], ref [163].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Pathways Connecting Adiposity to Breast Cancer Outcomes
subsections.subsection_title: Sex hormones and adipose-derived endocrine effects
subsections.content:
Adipose tissue is an active endocrine organ that can amplify estrogenic signaling, particularly after menopause when peripheral aromatization becomes the dominant source of estradiol. Aromatase expression is increased in adipose stromal cells and is further induced by prostaglandin E2 and inflammatory mediators, linking obesity to higher local and systemic estrogen exposure ref [164], ref [165]. In postmenopausal women, greater adiposity is consistently associated with higher circulating estradiol and estrone and lower sex hormone-binding globulin, thereby increasing bioavailable sex steroids that may promote hormone receptor-positive tumor growth and late recurrence ref [166], ref [167].

These endocrine effects are biologically plausible within the breast microenvironment itself. Breast adipose tissue adjacent to tumors can exhibit enhanced aromatase activity and inflammatory changes, including crown-like structures, creating a paracrine niche that sustains estrogen production and receptor signaling ref [168], ref [169]. Obesity may also alter progesterone-related and androgenic pathways, but the most reproducible prognostic signal has involved estrogens and reduced SHBG ref [166], ref [170]. Epidemiologic studies further support this framework: obesity is associated with higher risk of postmenopausal, estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer and with poorer outcomes in many cohorts, patterns compatible with adiposity-driven endocrine stimulation ref [171], ref [5].

Endocrine consequences of adiposity may also modify treatment response. In adjuvant endocrine therapy settings, obesity has been associated with less complete estrogen suppression during aromatase inhibition and, in some analyses, worse outcomes among women receiving aromatase inhibitors compared with tamoxifen ref [172], ref [173]. Trials and pooled analyses have similarly reported higher recurrence or mortality in patients with obesity despite standard systemic therapy, suggesting that host endocrine milieu may partially attenuate therapeutic benefit ref [139], ref [174]. More broadly, the obesity–breast cancer link summarized by major reviews and expert reports places sex steroid biology at the center of mechanistic models connecting body fatness with progression and survivorship ref [175], ref [176].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Pathways Connecting Adiposity to Breast Cancer Outcomes
subsections.content:
Excess adiposity is increasingly understood as a state of chronic, low-grade inflammation that can shape breast cancer progression. Hypertrophic adipocytes undergo stress and death, promoting macrophage recruitment and crown-like structures in mammary fat; these lesions are linked to local NF-kappaB activation, cyclooxygenase-2 signaling, and increased aromatase expression, thereby coupling inflammatory and endocrine mechanisms ref [177], ref [178], ref [179]. Obesity is also associated with elevated systemic inflammatory mediators including C-reactive protein, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, which have been associated with poorer breast cancer outcomes in several cohorts ref [180], ref [181], ref [182].

Beyond soluble mediators, obesity remodels antitumor immunity. In murine and translational studies, obesity promotes myeloid skewing, macrophage infiltration, and T-cell dysfunction, while inflammatory adipose-derived cytokines and chemokines can support angiogenesis, invasion, and metastatic seeding ref [183], ref [184], ref [185]. Leptin and other obesity-related signals may further enhance inflammatory crosstalk and immune suppression within the tumor microenvironment ref [186], ref [187]. These processes may be particularly relevant in aggressive subtypes such as triple-negative breast cancer, where obesity-associated inflammation has been linked to enhanced tumor-promoting stromal interactions ref [188].

Clinically, inflammatory biomarkers may partly mediate the adverse prognostic association of obesity, although causality and temporal ordering remain difficult to disentangle. Weight loss and physical activity can reduce circulating inflammatory markers in breast cancer survivors, suggesting that inflammation is potentially modifiable ref [189], ref [190]. More recently, obesity has also emerged as a context-dependent modifier of response to immune checkpoint blockade, underscoring the need to distinguish detrimental chronic inflammation from immune states that may alter therapeutic sensitivity ref [191].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Pathways Connecting Adiposity to Breast Cancer Outcomes
subsections.content:
Adipose tissue is an active endocrine organ whose secretome can remodel the breast tumor microenvironment. In obesity, hypertrophic adipocytes, cancer-associated adipocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and infiltrating myeloid cells generate a permissive niche characterized by altered extracellular matrix, oxidative stress, and reciprocal paracrine signaling with tumor cells ref [192], ref [193]. This shift is especially relevant in mammary tissue, where local adipocytes directly contact epithelial and malignant cells and can provide fatty acids and stromal mediators that support invasion and metabolic plasticity ref [194], ref [195].

Among adipokines, leptin has the strongest evidence for pro-tumorigenic activity. Leptin and its receptor are overexpressed in many breast cancers, and leptin signaling can enhance proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, stem-like traits, and crosstalk with estrogen, HER2, JAK/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, and inflammatory pathways ref [196], ref [197], ref [198], ref [199]. By contrast, adiponectin generally shows anti-proliferative and insulin-sensitizing effects, with lower circulating levels in obesity potentially removing a restraint on tumor growth; experimental studies indicate inhibition of mitogenic signaling and induction of apoptosis, although effects may vary by receptor context and subtype ref [200], ref [201].

Other adipose-derived mediators further shape the stromal and immune milieu. Resistin, visfatin/NAMPT, IL-6, CCL2, and autotaxin-lysophosphatidate signaling have been implicated in macrophage recruitment, inflammatory polarization, angiogenesis, and enhanced metastatic competence ref [202], ref [203], ref [204], ref [205]. Histologically, obesity-associated crown-like structures in breast adipose tissue mark macrophage-rich local inflammation and correlate with aromatase induction and a microenvironment favorable to progression ref [206]. Collectively, adipokine-driven reprogramming of the tumor microenvironment provides a plausible mechanistic link between adiposity and poorer breast cancer outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Pathways Connecting Adiposity to Breast Cancer Outcomes
subsections.subsection_title: Body composition, muscle loss, and functional reserve
subsections.content:
Body mass index incompletely captures the prognostic biology of adiposity because patients with the same BMI can differ markedly in skeletal muscle, visceral adiposity, and ectopic fat. Computed tomography–based studies in early and metastatic breast cancer show that low muscle mass and adverse muscle radiodensity are common even among individuals classified as overweight or obese, supporting the concept of sarcopenic obesity as a clinically relevant phenotype rather than a simple extension of BMI-defined obesity ref [207], ref [208], ref [7]. In population studies, obesity itself is associated with reduced relative muscle mass and poorer physical function, suggesting that excess adiposity may erode physiologic reserve before or during cancer treatment ref [209], ref [210].

Loss of muscle and functional reserve may worsen breast cancer outcomes through several linked mechanisms. Skeletal muscle is a major regulator of glucose disposal and systemic insulin sensitivity; reduced muscle mass therefore amplifies metabolic dysregulation, while intramuscular lipid accumulation and poor muscle quality may further promote inflammation and frailty ref [211], ref [212]. In oncology cohorts, sarcopenia has been associated with inferior survival and greater treatment toxicity across tumor types, and in breast cancer specifically low muscle mass has been linked to chemotherapy toxicity, lower dose intensity, and worse prognosis ref [208], ref [213], ref [214], ref [215]. Functional decline is also important: poorer cardiorespiratory fitness and lower exercise capacity predict morbidity and mortality in breast cancer survivorship, indicating that host reserve modifies the ability to tolerate disease and therapy ref [216], ref [217].

These observations suggest that body composition is both a mediator and a modifier of the adiposity–outcome relationship. Weight gain after diagnosis may preferentially increase fat while treatment, inactivity, ovarian suppression, and aging accelerate muscle loss, creating a mismatch between body size and physiologic resilience ref [218], ref [219]. Accordingly, prognostic assessment may be improved by integrating CT-derived muscle and adipose measures with functional metrics such as strength or exercise capacity, rather than relying on BMI alone ref [7], ref [217], ref [220].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Pathways Connecting Adiposity to Breast Cancer Outcomes
subsections.content:
Adiposity can modify both the delivery and biological efficacy of breast cancer therapy. In chemotherapy, concerns that body surface area–based dosing may be reduced in patients with obesity led to evidence reviews showing that full weight-based dosing is generally appropriate and that empiric dose capping can compromise outcomes without clearly reducing toxicity ref [221], ref [222]. Observational studies in adjuvant settings further linked higher BMI with lower pathologic complete response rates, particularly in some neoadjuvant regimens, suggesting that obesity-related pharmacokinetic, stromal, and metabolic factors may contribute to relative treatment resistance ref [223], ref [224].

Interactions are especially prominent for endocrine therapy. Aromatase inhibitor efficacy may be attenuated in women with obesity because adipose tissue remains a major site of aromatization and may sustain residual estrogen exposure despite treatment ref [225], ref [226]. Consistent with this biology, several adjuvant analyses reported worse outcomes for obese women receiving aromatase inhibitors, whereas the association appeared weaker or less consistent with tamoxifen ref [227], ref [228]. Obesity is also associated with treatment-related toxicities and altered supportive care needs, including greater risk of anthracycline- or trastuzumab-associated cardiac dysfunction and a higher baseline burden of comorbidity that can limit treatment intensity ref [229], ref [230].

Body composition may also interact with newer therapies. Sarcopenia and excess adiposity have been associated with greater chemotherapy toxicity and poorer tolerance, even when BMI alone is uninformative ref [231], ref [232]. For immunotherapy, obesity may simultaneously promote chronic inflammation and T-cell dysfunction yet, in some tumor types, correlate with altered checkpoint inhibitor responses; in breast cancer this remains biologically plausible but clinically unresolved ref [233]. Weight change during systemic therapy adds another layer, as treatment-induced gain in fat mass and loss of lean mass may worsen insulin resistance, functional reserve, and long-term survivorship outcomes ref [234], ref [235].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Issues in Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Prognostic Research
subsections.content:
Prognostic epidemiology on postdiagnosis body fatness relies predominantly on observational cohorts because randomization to adiposity is infeasible. Core design choices include inception cohorts assembled near diagnosis, survivorship cohorts recruited after completion of primary therapy, and analyses nested within clinical trial populations; each trades off internal validity, generalizability, and susceptibility to selection on survival [1,2]. Reporting frameworks specific to tumor-marker and prognostic studies have emphasized transparent specification of source population, time origin, eligibility, and outcome definitions because ambiguity in these elements can materially alter risk estimates [3,4].

A central issue is alignment of exposure assessment with the prognostic time scale. Studies that define follow-up from diagnosis but measure weight months or years later risk immortal-time and left-truncation biases unless delayed entry is handled appropriately [5,6]. Landmark and time-updated approaches can reduce bias when repeated postdiagnosis anthropometry is available, and multistate or competing-risk methods are often preferable because breast cancer recurrence, breast cancer death, and non-cancer death are distinct endpoints with different associations to adiposity [7,8]. Recommendations for prediction and prognosis research further stress adequate handling of censoring, missing data, and overfitting, especially when body size is modeled jointly with clinicopathologic factors [9,10].

Design-specific threats also shape interpretation. Trial cohorts may offer standardized treatment and outcome ascertainment but can be less representative than population-based cohorts [2,11]. Retrospective record-linkage studies are efficient yet vulnerable to incomplete covariate capture, whereas prospective cohorts better support confounder measurement and repeated exposure assessment [12]. More broadly, modern causal frameworks for prognosis caution against conditioning on postbaseline intermediates and advocate explicit estimands, target trial emulation where relevant, and sensitivity analyses for informative loss to follow-up and survivor bias [13,14].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Issues in Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Prognostic Research
subsections.content:
Exposure assessment is a central source of heterogeneity in studies of postdiagnosis body fatness and breast cancer prognosis. Most cohorts rely on body mass index (BMI), yet BMI is an imperfect proxy for adiposity because it does not distinguish fat from lean mass or capture fat distribution, a limitation emphasized in clinical and epidemiologic discussions of obesity metrics ref [3], ref [248]. Central adiposity may be more biologically relevant than BMI for insulin resistance, inflammation, and sex-steroid pathways; accordingly, waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio can provide complementary information, although they are measured less consistently in oncology cohorts ref [249], ref [250]. Body composition methods such as dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, bioimpedance, and computed tomography are more informative for visceral fat and sarcopenic obesity, but are rarely available at scale and often restricted to selected clinical samples ref [251], ref [252].

Misclassification also arises from when and how weight is measured. Self-reported height and weight systematically underestimate BMI, with differential error by sex, age, and adiposity level, potentially attenuating dose-response estimates ref [253], ref [254]. In breast cancer cohorts, postdiagnosis measures may be obtained during surgery, chemotherapy, or survivorship follow-up, periods characterized by fluid shifts and treatment-related changes that reduce comparability across studies ref [255], ref [256]. Single measurements further obscure trajectories; repeated-weight studies show substantial variation in gain and loss after diagnosis, suggesting that time-varying exposure models are preferable to fixed classifications ref [235], ref [99].

Analytically, nondifferential measurement error in adiposity markers generally biases associations toward the null, but differential ascertainment by disease severity, treatment, or recurrence surveillance can produce more complex bias. Where possible, reviews should distinguish measured from self-reported anthropometry, prediagnosis from postdiagnosis exposure windows, and global from central or imaging-based adiposity phenotypes. Validation or calibration approaches, and harmonization efforts such as the Body Fatness and Breast Cancer Survival Collaborative Group, can improve comparability and interpretation of pooled estimates ref [254], ref [257], ref [258].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Issues in Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Prognostic Research
subsections.subsection_title: Reverse causation and illness-related weight change
subsections.content:
Reverse causation is a central threat in studies of postdiagnosis adiposity and breast cancer prognosis because weight loss after diagnosis may reflect occult recurrence, progressive disease, treatment toxicity, sarcopenia, or systemic inflammation rather than a causal effect of lower body fatness on survival. Cancer cachexia is characterized by involuntary loss of weight and skeletal muscle driven by metabolic and inflammatory perturbations, making declining body weight a potential marker of poor prognosis rather than a protective exposure ref [1], ref [2]. In breast cancer cohorts, substantial postdiagnosis weight change is common during and after treatment, but gain and loss may arise from distinct mechanisms and therefore should not be interpreted symmetrically ref [3], ref [4].

Methodologically, analyses that relate recent weight change to recurrence or mortality are especially vulnerable when exposure assessment occurs close to the event, when prevalent rather than incident survivors are enrolled, or when follow-up begins before completion of primary therapy. Landmark analyses, lagged exposure definitions, exclusion of events occurring soon after weight measurement, and explicit separation of intentional from unintentional weight loss can reduce bias, although intent is often poorly measured ref [5], ref [6], ref [7]. Repeated measures are particularly important because single postdiagnosis weights obscure trajectories and may misclassify temporary treatment-related fluctuations, including chemotherapy-associated gain, edema, or endocrine-therapy-related changes ref [8], ref [9].

Interpretation also requires attention to body composition. Weight loss in survivors may preferentially represent depletion of lean mass, and sarcopenia or sarcopenic obesity has been associated with worse outcomes independent of BMI, reinforcing that crude body weight change can conflate prognostically adverse wasting with reductions in adiposity ref [10], ref [11], ref [12]. Recommendations from cancer survivorship guidance therefore emphasize avoiding weight loss during active treatment unless clinically indicated and evaluating unexplained postdiagnosis weight decline as a possible manifestation of illness burden rather than evidence of benefit ref [13], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Issues in Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Prognostic Research
subsections.content:
In studies of postdiagnosis adiposity and breast cancer outcomes, confounding is substantial because body fatness is patterned by age, menopausal status, stage, comorbidity, smoking, physical activity, socioeconomic position, and treatment receipt, all of which also predict prognosis. Methodological work in prognostic research emphasizes that inappropriate covariate selection can either leave residual confounding or induce bias through overadjustment and conditioning on colliders ref [259], ref [260], ref [261]. Directed acyclic graph approaches are therefore useful for distinguishing pre-exposure confounders from variables on the causal pathway or common effects ref [262], ref [263].

A central challenge is separating total effects of adiposity from mediated effects through tumor characteristics, metabolic dysfunction, treatment dosing, and treatment adherence. Adjusting for stage, subtype, chemotherapy dose intensity, endocrine therapy use, or recurrence-related intermediates may attenuate biologically relevant pathways rather than control confounding. Contemporary mediation frameworks based on counterfactual definitions clarify decomposition into direct and indirect effects, but require strong assumptions about no unmeasured exposure-mediator and mediator-outcome confounding, assumptions that are rarely fully satisfied in oncology cohorts ref [264], ref [265], ref [266], ref [267]. Time-varying confounding is especially problematic when weight change after diagnosis both influences and is influenced by treatment and health status; g-methods such as marginal structural models were developed for precisely this setting ref [268], ref [269].

Effect modification should be examined rather than treated as nuisance heterogeneity. Biological and clinical rationale exists for variation by menopausal status, hormone receptor status, molecular subtype, race/ethnicity, baseline obesity, diabetes, and systemic treatment, and pooled analyses have reported stronger adverse associations of obesity for all-cause mortality than for breast-cancer-specific mortality and variation across estrogen receptor strata ref [270], ref [271]. Methodological guidance recommends evaluating interaction on clearly defined additive or multiplicative scales, prespecifying subgroup hypotheses, and avoiding interpretation of underpowered subgroup contrasts as definitive evidence ref [272], ref [273].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Issues in Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Prognostic Research
subsections.content:
Meta-analysis of postdiagnosis adiposity and breast cancer prognosis must accommodate substantial between-study heterogeneity arising from differences in outcome definitions, timing of body fatness assessment, covariate control, and whether effect estimates are reported as categories, linear contrasts, or splines. Random-effects models are therefore generally preferable to fixed-effect synthesis, but their assumptions and small-study behavior should be made explicit, especially when the number of studies is limited or heterogeneity is large ref [274], ref [275], ref [276]. Quantification with tau-squared and prediction intervals can be more informative than reliance on I-squared alone ref [277], ref [278].

Because body mass index and other adiposity measures are often categorized inconsistently, dose-response meta-analysis is especially valuable. One-stage or two-stage generalized least-squares approaches permit estimation of linear and non-linear associations while using the full information from exposure categories and correlated log-risk estimates ref [279], ref [280], ref [281]. Non-linearity should be examined because prognostic associations may differ at low versus high adiposity, and because illness-related weight loss can distort the lower tail of the distribution.

Exploration of heterogeneity should be prespecified and guided by causal and clinical considerations, including menopausal status, tumor subtype, treatment era, geography, follow-up length, and adjustment for stage, comorbidity, and smoking. Subgroup analysis and meta-regression are useful but vulnerable to ecological bias and low power ref [282], ref [283]. Selective reporting and publication bias should be assessed cautiously using contour-enhanced funnel plots or regression-based tests, recognizing their limited interpretability in sparse and heterogeneous prognostic literatures ref [284], ref [285]. When individual participant data are available, IPD meta-analysis can harmonize exposure definitions, model time-varying effects, and address competing risks more rigorously than aggregate-data synthesis ref [286], ref [287].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Issues in Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Prognostic Research
subsections.subsection_title: Quality assessment and certainty of evidence
subsections.content:
Quality appraisal in prognostic reviews of postdiagnosis body fatness and breast cancer outcomes should move beyond reporting checklists and address domain-specific risks of bias. For prognosis studies, QUIPS provides a useful framework spanning study participation, attrition, prognostic factor measurement, outcome measurement, confounding, and statistical analysis/reporting ref [288]. Broader guidance from PROGRESS also emphasizes that prognostic factor research requires explicit attention to time origin, outcome definition, model specification, and validation ref [289], ref [290]. In observational nutrition and obesity research, these domains are especially salient because body fatness may be assessed at diagnosis, after treatment, or by recalled prediagnosis weight, with variable susceptibility to measurement error and selective survival.

Certainty of evidence is harder to judge than in intervention reviews because associations may be distorted by residual confounding, reverse causation, and informative weight change. GRADE has been adapted for prognosis questions, but application requires careful consideration of phase of investigation, consistency of effect direction, and whether dose-response patterns are robust to bias-sensitive analyses ref [291], ref [292]. Reviews should therefore integrate structured risk-of-bias tools developed specifically for non-randomized studies, such as ROBINS-I and the later ROBINS-E framework for environmental and exposure studies, while recognizing that these tools were not designed solely for prognostic factor questions ref [293], ref [294]. Recent work on target trial emulation further highlights how explicit causal specification can sharpen judgments about comparability, immortal time, and selection biases in postdiagnosis exposure analyses ref [295].

In practice, certainty should usually be rated down when studies inadequately handle prediagnosis adiposity, stage, treatment, comorbidity, smoking, and physical activity, or when they condition on mediators such as recurrence treatment pathways. Selective reporting and small-study effects also warrant scrutiny; recommendations from MOOSE, PRISMA 2020, and reporting guidance for tumor marker/prognostic studies underscore transparent protocoling, complete effect reporting, and clear handling of multiplicity ref [296], ref [297], ref [238], ref [298]. Where quantitative synthesis is pursued, reviewers should distinguish low certainty caused by biased primary evidence from statistical imprecision alone, and should present summary judgments by outcome and exposure metric rather than a single global rating ref [299], ref [300].

subsections.section_title: Global Patterns, Equity Considerations, and Translation to Survivorship Practice
subsections.content:
The global cancer burden is rising in both incidence and survivorship, with marked geographic heterogeneity driven by demographic transition, changing risk-factor profiles, and uneven health-system capacity. Contemporary estimates from GLOBOCAN 2020 indicate substantial regional variation in the incidence and mortality of common cancers, while projections suggest further growth concentrated in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) as populations age and diagnosis expands ref [301], ref [302]. Long-term survivorship is therefore no longer confined to high-income settings; instead, it is increasingly a worldwide phenomenon shaped by differences in stage at diagnosis, treatment availability, and competing non-cancer mortality ref [303], ref [304].

Regional patterns also reflect distinct epidemiologic transitions. In many high-income countries, declining smoking prevalence and improvements in early detection and treatment have shifted survivorship toward longer-term management of treatment sequelae and comorbidity, whereas several LMICs continue to face a dual burden of infection-related cancers and rapidly increasing obesity-associated malignancies ref [305], ref [306], ref [307]. The rising contribution of high body-mass index to cancer burden has been documented globally, but its magnitude varies by sex, region, and development level, with particularly fast increases in parts of Latin America, the Middle East, North Africa, and some Pacific settings ref [308], ref [309].

These differences have direct implications for survivorship practice. Regions with high survival after breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers may prioritize risk-stratified follow-up, rehabilitation, and management of metabolic late effects, while settings with later-stage presentation or limited oncology infrastructure require models that integrate survivorship with essential primary care and chronic disease services ref [43], ref [310]. International survivorship planning must therefore be calibrated to local cancer profiles, treatment exposures, and background burdens of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease rather than extrapolated uncritically from North American or European cohorts ref [311], ref [312], ref [313].

subsections.section_title: Global Patterns, Equity Considerations, and Translation to Survivorship Practice
subsections.content:
Equity is a central concern in cancer survivorship because the burden of obesity, treatment-related metabolic dysfunction, and limited access to supportive care is patterned by social disadvantage. In the United States, racial/ethnic minority groups and people with lower income are less likely to receive guideline-concordant survivorship care and more likely to report unmet physical and psychosocial needs, with implications for weight management and cardiometabolic risk reduction after treatment ref [314], ref [315]. Similar gradients are seen internationally, where social determinants, health-system fragmentation, and out-of-pocket costs constrain uptake of rehabilitation, nutrition counseling, and physical activity programs ref [316], ref [317].

Vulnerable populations include rural survivors, older adults, migrants, Indigenous peoples, and those with multimorbidity or disability, for whom distance, digital exclusion, language barriers, and competing life demands limit participation in lifestyle interventions ref [318], ref [319], ref [320]. Adolescents and young adults also face distinctive barriers related to interrupted education, employment insecurity, and long-term treatment toxicity ref [321]. These inequities intersect with biologic and clinical heterogeneity: obesity prevalence and its sequelae are often higher in groups already exposed to structural racism and neighborhood deprivation, amplifying disparities in survivorship outcomes ref [322], ref [323].

Accordingly, survivorship models should move beyond one-size-fits-all delivery toward culturally tailored, low-cost, and community-linked approaches, including patient navigation, telehealth with attention to the digital divide, and integration of social needs screening into oncology follow-up ref [324], ref [325]. The broader equity literature further supports proportionate universalism: interventions should be offered universally, but with intensity and resources matched to need so that survivorship care does not inadvertently widen disparities ref [326], ref [327].

subsections.section_title: Global Patterns, Equity Considerations, and Translation to Survivorship Practice
subsections.content:
Current survivorship guidelines increasingly converge on the principle that body weight, diet, and physical activity should be addressed as core components of post-treatment care, while recognizing heterogeneity in treatment sequelae, comorbidity, and recurrence risk. Major guidance from the American Cancer Society, the American Society of Clinical Oncology, and the American College of Sports Medicine supports routine assessment of weight status, counseling on healthy dietary patterns, and promotion of regular physical activity as part of survivorship care planning rather than as optional adjuncts ref [63], ref [15], ref [328], ref [329]. These recommendations are reinforced by evidence syntheses linking adiposity and low activity to poorer cancer-specific and overall outcomes in several survivor populations ref [330], ref [331], ref [332].

For guideline development, the main implication is a shift from generic lifestyle advice to risk-stratified, implementation-oriented pathways. Survivorship recommendations should specify when to screen for weight gain, sarcopenic obesity, metabolic syndrome, fatigue, and functional limitations; when to refer to dietitians, exercise professionals, or behavioral programs; and how to adapt advice for treatment-related cardiometabolic risk, lymphedema, neuropathy, ostomies, or endocrine therapy ref [328], ref [333], ref [334], ref [335]. Guidance should also acknowledge that intentional weight loss may be appropriate for some survivors with overweight or obesity, but requires individualized monitoring to preserve lean mass and physical function, particularly in older adults and those exposed to intensive systemic therapy ref [336], ref [337].

Guidelines should further emphasize equitable delivery and long-term follow-up. Endorsements of healthy lifestyle behaviors are unlikely to reduce disparities unless paired with pragmatic recommendations on culturally tailored counseling, telehealth or community-based models, reimbursement, and minimum datasets for monitoring adherence and outcomes ref [338], ref [339]. Integration with survivorship care plans and implementation frameworks can help translate efficacy evidence into scalable practice, while highlighting areas where recommendations remain conditional because trial evidence for recurrence and survival endpoints is still evolving ref [15], ref [329], ref [340].

subsections.section_title: Global Patterns, Equity Considerations, and Translation to Survivorship Practice
subsections.subsection_title: Lifestyle intervention and weight management strategies
subsections.content:
Lifestyle interventions are a pragmatic bridge between survivorship care and chronic disease prevention, particularly where excess adiposity, sarcopenic obesity, fatigue, and cardiometabolic comorbidity co-occur after treatment. Observational evidence has linked postdiagnosis physical activity and healthier dietary patterns with lower mortality and recurrence in several cancers, especially breast and colorectal cancer, supporting weight management as part of broader survivorship risk reduction rather than as a cosmetic goal alone ref [341], ref [342], ref [343], ref [344].

Randomized trials indicate that structured exercise can improve physical function, fatigue, and quality of life during and after treatment, while multicomponent diet-plus-activity programs can achieve modest but clinically meaningful weight loss in overweight survivors ref [328], ref [345], ref [346], ref [347]. Large pragmatic studies in breast cancer survivors, including the ENERGY and LISA trials, showed that telephone- or group-based behavioral programs can produce sustained but attenuating weight loss, highlighting both feasibility and the challenge of long-term maintenance ref [348], ref [349]. For breast cancer-related lymphedema, carefully progressed resistance training appears safe and may reduce symptom burden, countering earlier concerns that strength training should be avoided ref [350].

Current strategies therefore favor individualized, culturally adapted interventions that combine caloric moderation, diet quality, aerobic and resistance exercise, and behavioral support, with delivery through clinic, community, or digital platforms according to local resources ref [351], ref [352]. Guideline statements from the American Cancer Society and the American College of Sports Medicine converge on regular physical activity, limiting weight gain, and referral pathways for nutrition and exercise specialists, although evidence for intentional weight loss improving hard oncologic endpoints remains incomplete and is being directly tested in trials such as BWEL ref [15], ref [353].

subsections.section_title: Global Patterns, Equity Considerations, and Translation to Survivorship Practice
subsections.content:
Key evidence gaps concern causal inference, exposure measurement, and representativeness. Much of the survivorship literature remains observational, with heterogeneous definitions of adiposity, weight change, diet, and physical activity, limiting comparability across studies and meta-analyses. Consensus statements have repeatedly called for harmonized core outcomes, stronger assessment of body composition and sarcopenic obesity, and better characterization of treatment exposures and comorbidity, rather than reliance on body mass index alone ref [63], ref [64], ref [120]. Important methodological priorities include prospective repeated-measures designs, use of causal frameworks to address time-varying confounding, and incorporation of implementation-relevant outcomes such as adherence, toxicity, and quality of life ref [246], ref [354].

A second gap is external validity. Data are dominated by breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer cohorts from high-income countries, whereas evidence for survivors in low- and middle-income settings, younger adults, older adults with multimorbidity, and racially or ethnically marginalized populations remains sparse. Global cancer control reports and survivorship commissions emphasize that research must move beyond efficacy toward equitable delivery, including financial toxicity, access barriers, and culturally adapted intervention models ref [316], ref [310], ref [355]. Trials also need sufficient power to examine effect modification by sex, menopausal status, treatment type, stage, and social disadvantage, because pooled lifestyle recommendations may obscure clinically relevant heterogeneity ref [329], ref [352].

Research priorities therefore include pragmatic multicenter trials of weight management and physical activity embedded in oncology care, linkage of survivorship cohorts to registries and electronic health records, and integration of biomarkers, patient-reported outcomes, and digital phenotyping. Recent guidance for exercise-oncology trials, survivorship research, and implementation science provides a roadmap for standardized intervention reporting, hybrid effectiveness-implementation designs, and scalable models that can be adapted across resource settings ref [328], ref [356], ref [357], ref [358]. Long-term follow-up is especially needed to determine whether post-diagnosis lifestyle change alters recurrence, second primary cancers, cardiovascular outcomes, and overall survival, not only intermediate endpoints ref [359].

subsections.section_title: Global Patterns, Equity Considerations, and Translation to Survivorship Practice
subsections.subsection_title: Integration with cancer prevention and control frameworks
subsections.content:
Evidence on adiposity, physical activity, diet, and metabolic health in survivors should be embedded within comprehensive cancer control frameworks rather than treated as an isolated survivorship issue. The World Health Organization position on cancer prevention and control and the European Code Against Cancer both emphasize common lifestyle determinants across the cancer continuum, creating a policy basis for linking survivorship services with population-level prevention, early detection, and chronic disease management ref [360], ref [361]. This alignment is reinforced by major prevention syntheses showing that excess body fatness, inactivity, alcohol use, and poor diet influence both primary cancer risk and downstream outcomes after diagnosis ref [136], ref [64].

A practical implication is that survivorship care plans can serve as a delivery platform for risk-stratified prevention: assessment of weight change, comorbidity, treatment-related cardiometabolic risk, and health behaviors can be paired with referral pathways to tobacco cessation, exercise, nutrition, and obesity services already used in noncommunicable disease programs ref [43], ref [362]. Guidance from the American Cancer Society, ASCO, and the World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research supports this convergence by recommending physical activity, healthy dietary patterns, and weight management as core elements of survivorship care ref [15], ref [363], ref [364].

Integration also requires implementation frameworks that account for multilevel barriers. The Lancet Oncology Commission on cancer survivorship and rehabilitation argues for survivorship to be incorporated into universal health coverage and national cancer control plans, while implementation science frameworks such as RE-AIM and the WHO health-system building blocks can help adapt interventions to local workforce, financing, and information-system constraints ref [365], ref [366], ref [367]. In low-resource settings, this favors task-sharing, primary-care follow-up, and digital or community-based models that connect survivorship support to broader cancer control and NCD strategies ref [368], ref [369].
